correctness.rationale: For consecutive points (a,b,z),(b,a,w), eliminating z,w gives the reduced residuals K_1=b(m+z)-Aa and K_2=a(m+w)-Ab, with z=α(a²+rb²)/(1-r²) and w=α(b²+ra²)/(1-r²). A=1-n>0 makes zero coordinates yield the origin; a=b gives a fixed point and a=-b≠0 gives the unique symmetric cycle exactly under the first strict inequality. For Δ=a²-b²≠0, aK_1-bK_2=Δ(-A+αab/(1+r)) and bK_1-aK_2=-Δ(m+αr(a²+b²)/(1-r²)); the row transformation has determinant -Δ, so the sum/product constraints are necessary and sufficient. Positive distinct squared roots exist iff S>2|B|, with just two reflected orbits after quotient by phase. At equality the roots coincide. An independent derivative check: eliminate the third coordinate from F²-I by first using residual rows for the two second-coordinate equations and the third-coordinate return; subtract multiples of the first row to account for the intermediate second coordinate a+K_1 instead of a. The scalar Schur factor from the third-coordinate return is r²-1, giving det(P-I)=(r²-1)det DK. Differentiating the two factorizations at an asymmetric zero yields det DK=-2rΔ²/((1+r)(1-r²)), hence the asserted identity. The real monic characteristic polynomial is negative at 1 and positive at large arguments. The threshold difference for α=1 is A(1-3r)/(1-r), and for α=-1 the two thresholds are strictly ordered for every admissible r. The strict endpoints and the square-root discriminant onset both agree.

More directly, from any A>0 to any A'=sA>0, scale (a,b) by sqrt(s) and (z,w,m) by s. This bijects all return solutions, preserves primitive period and scales thresholds by s. Under this change K' evaluated at scaled coordinates is s^(3/2)K, so det DK' scales by s²; the third-coordinate Schur factor r²-1 is unchanged. The prior determinant scales by exactly the same s² as (a²-b²)². Choose A' in (1,2) for the earlier parameter range.
The sign-flip second-iterate duality transfers the asymmetric result to the negative sign, and the discriminant S²-4B² already gives the onset expansion using the earlier sum/product equations.
